column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 15: Speak good or keep silent; honour the neighbour and the guest

column2: Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day,

let him say what is good or keep silent. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest.” Al-Bukhārī and Muslim reported it.

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded this hadith through several routes from Abū Hurayrah. Some of its wordings have “let him not harm his neighbour”, some have “let him host his guest well”, and some have “let him maintain his ties of kinship” in place of the mention of the neighbour.
They also recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of Abū Shurayḥ al-Khuzāʿī, from the Prophet ﷺ.
This hadith has also been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, Ibn ʿAbbās and other Companions.
His words ﷺ, “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him do such-and-such,” show that these traits are among the traits of faith.

We have already seen that deeds are included in faith. The Prophet ﷺ explained faith as patience and generosity of spirit (samāḥah), and al-Ḥasan said: What is meant is patience in keeping away from sins, and generosity of spirit in acts of obedience.
The deeds of faith sometimes concern the rights of Allah, such as carrying out obligations and leaving what is forbidden; saying what is good, and otherwise keeping silent, is one of these.

At other times they concern the rights of His servants, such as honouring the guest, honouring the neighbour and refraining from harming him. These, then, are three things the believer is commanded to do. The first is to say what is good and otherwise keep silent. Al-Ṭabarānī narrated, from the hadith of Aswad ibn Aṣram al-Muḥāribī, that he said:
I said: O Messenger of Allah, give me some advice. He said: “Do you control your tongue?”
I said: What do I control, if I do not control my tongue?
He said: “Do you control your hand?”
I said: What do I control, if I do not control my hand?
He said: “Then say nothing with your tongue but what is right, and stretch out your hand only to what is good.”

It has come that uprightness of the tongue is one of the traits of faith, as in the Musnad, from Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ: “A servant's faith is not upright until his heart is upright, and his heart is not upright until his tongue is upright.”

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “A servant does not attain the reality of faith until he holds back his tongue.” Al-Ṭabarānī also recorded, from the hadith of Muʿādh ibn Jabal, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“You will remain safe as long as you keep silent; when you speak, it is written either for you or against you.”
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever keeps silent is saved.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “A man may speak a word without considering what is in it, and by it slip into the Fire farther than the distance between the east and the west.”
Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“A man may speak a word in which he sees no harm, and by it plunge seventy autumns into the Fire.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“A man may speak a word that pleases Allah, paying it no heed, and Allah raises him by degrees for it; and a servant may speak a word that angers Allah, paying it no heed, and by it plunge into Hell.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Sulaymān ibn Suḥaym, from his mother, that she said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “A man may come so near to Paradise that there is only a cubit between him and it; then he speaks a word, and is driven farther from it than Ṣanʿāʾ.”

Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Bilāl ibn al-Ḥārith, that he said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “One of you may speak a word that pleases Allah, never imagining it will go as far as it does,

and Allah records for him by it His good pleasure until the day he meets Him; and one of you may speak a word that angers Allah, never imagining it will go as far as it does, and Allah records against him by it His anger until the day he meets Him.”

We cited earlier the hadith of Umm Ḥabībah, from the Prophet ﷺ: “All the speech of the son of Ādam counts against him, not for him, except enjoining good, forbidding evil, and the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.”

His words ﷺ, “let him say what is good or keep silent”, command saying what is good and keeping silent about anything else. This shows that there is no speech for which speaking and keeping silent are equal;
rather, either it is good, and one is commanded to say it, or it is not good, and one is commanded to keep silent about it. The hadiths of Muʿādh and Umm Ḥabībah point to this.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded the hadith of Muʿādh ibn Jabal with the wording that the Prophet ﷺ said to him: “Muʿādh, may your mother lose you! Do you say anything that does not count either for you or against you?”

Allah the Exalted has said: “When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left, he utters no word but there is a watcher with him, ever present” [Qāf 50:17–18]. The righteous Salaf were unanimous that the one on his right records good deeds
and the one on his left records evil deeds. This has also been narrated as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ) from the hadith of Abū Umāmah, with a weak chain.
In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from the Prophet ﷺ: “When one of you is praying, he is in intimate converse with his Lord, and the angel is on his right.”
It has been narrated as marfūʿ from the hadith of Ḥudhayfah: “On his right is the recorder of good deeds.”
They differed over whether the recording angel writes down everything a person says, or only what carries reward or punishment.
There are two well-known views.
ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah said, from Ibn ʿAbbās: He records everything a person says, good or bad, even his saying “I ate,” “I drank,” “I went,” “I came,”

until, on Thursday, his words and deeds are presented, and whatever good or bad is in them is kept and the rest is discarded. That is the meaning of the words of the Exalted: “Allah erases what He wills and confirms [what He wills], and with Him is the Mother of the Book” [al-Raʿd 13:39].

Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: A man was riding a donkey, and it stumbled with him, and he said: May the donkey perish! The companion on the right said: That is not a good deed for me to record. The companion on the left said:

It is not one of the evil deeds for me to record. So Allah revealed to the companion on the left: Whatever the companion on the right leaves, record it. So the angel entered “May the donkey perish!” among the evil deeds.
The apparent sense of this is that whatever is not a good deed is an evil deed, even if one is not punished for it; for some evil deeds may go unpunished

and may be expiated by avoiding the major sins. But the person has lost the time spent on them, since it went to waste, and so on the Day of Resurrection he will feel regret and sorrow over it, which is a kind of punishment.

Imam Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “No people rise from a gathering in which they did not remember Allah but they rise from something like the carcass of a donkey, and it will be a cause of regret for them.”

Al-Tirmidhī recorded it with the wording: “No people sit in a gathering in which they do not remember Allah or send blessings on their Prophet but it will be a liability against them; if He wills, He will punish them, and if He wills, He will forgive them.”

In a narration of Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī: “Whoever sits somewhere without remembering Allah there, it will be a liability against him from Allah; and whoever lies down somewhere without remembering Allah there,
it will be a liability against him from Allah.” Al-Nasāʾī added: “And whoever stands somewhere without remembering Allah there, it will be a liability against him from Allah.”

Al-Nasāʾī also recorded, from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “No people sit in a gathering in which they do not remember Allah but it will be a cause of regret for them on the Day of Resurrection, even if they enter Paradise.”

Mujāhid said: No people sit in a gathering and disperse before remembering Allah but they disperse from something fouler than the stench of a carcass, and their gathering bears witness against them for their heedlessness;

and no people sit in a gathering and remember Allah before they disperse but they disperse from something sweeter than the scent of musk, and their gathering bears witness for them for their remembrance.

One of the Salaf said: On the Day of Resurrection the hours of a person's life will be shown to him, and for every hour that passed him in which he did not remember Allah, his soul will be torn to pieces with regret.

Al-Ṭabarānī recorded it as marfūʿ from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah: “No hour passes the son of Ādam in which he does not remember Allah with good but he will feel regret over it on the Day of Resurrection.”
From this it is clear that, where speech is not good, silence is better than speaking — except for what need calls for and cannot be done without.

It has been narrated that Ibn Masʿūd said: Beware of superfluous speech; it is enough for a man to say what meets his need. Al-Nakhaʿī said: People are ruined by superfluous wealth and superfluous speech.
Moreover, much speech that is not needed hardens the heart, as in al-Tirmidhī, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar as marfūʿ:
“Do not speak much without the remembrance of Allah, for much speech without the remembrance of Allah hardens the heart, and the farthest of people from Allah is the hard heart.”
ʿUmar said: Whoever speaks much makes many slips; whoever makes many slips has many sins; and whoever has many sins, the Fire is more fitting for him.
Al-ʿUqaylī recorded it as marfūʿ from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, with a weak chain.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān said: Speech is of four kinds only: that you remember Allah, recite the Qurʾān, are asked about some knowledge and give the answer, or speak about the worldly matters that concern you.
A man said to Salmān: Give me some advice. He said: Do not speak. The man said: No one who lives among people can manage not to speak. He said: Then if you speak, speak the truth, or keep quiet.
Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) used to take hold of his tongue and say: This is what has brought me to perilous places.
Ibn Masʿūd said: By Allah, besides whom there is no god, nothing on earth more deserves a long imprisonment than the tongue.
Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The sages are agreed that the head of wisdom is silence.
Shumayṭ ibn ʿAjlān said: Son of Ādam, as long as you are silent you are safe; but when you speak, be on your guard: it is either for you or against you.
This is a subject that would take long to cover fully.

The point is that the Prophet ﷺ commanded us to speak what is good and to keep silent about what is not. Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Ḥibbān recorded, from the hadith of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, that a man said: O Messenger of Allah, teach me a deed that will admit me into Paradise — and he mentioned the hadith, in which the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Then feed the hungry, give water to the thirsty, enjoin good and forbid evil, and hold your tongue from evil. If you cannot manage that, then hold back your tongue except from good.”

Speech, then, is not commanded unconditionally, and neither is silence; rather, one must speak what is good and keep silent about what is evil. The Salaf often praised keeping silent about evil and about what does not concern one,
because it is hard on the soul, which is why people so often fall into it. They used to work on their souls and struggle with them to keep silent about what did not concern them.

Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: No Ḥajj, no guarding the frontier and no jihād is harder than restraining the tongue. If you woke each morning anxious about your tongue, you would wake in great distress. He also said: Imprisoning the tongue is the believer's prison; if you woke each morning anxious about your tongue, you would wake in great distress.

Ibn al-Mubārak was asked about Luqmān's saying to his son, "If speech is of silver, silence is of gold," and he said: It means that if speaking in obedience to Allah is silver, then keeping silent rather than disobeying Allah is gold.
This comes back to the point that refraining from sins is better than doing acts of obedience, which has already been discussed in full.
People were discussing in the presence of al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays which is better, silence or speech.
Some said: Silence is better. Al-Aḥnaf said: Speech is better,
because the merit of silence goes no further than the one who keeps it, while good speech benefits whoever hears it.
One of the scholars said in the presence of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (may Allah have mercy on him): The one who keeps silent with knowledge is like the one who speaks with knowledge. ʿUmar said:

I hope that the one who speaks with knowledge will be the better of the two in rank on the Day of Resurrection, because his benefit goes to people, whereas the other's silence is for himself. The man said to him: Commander of the Believers, what about the trial that speaking brings?
At that ʿUmar wept bitterly.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz once gave a sermon, and the people were moved and wept, so he broke off his sermon. He was told: If you had finished what you were saying, we would have hoped that Allah would bring benefit through it. ʿUmar said: Speech is a trial, and action is worthier of the believer than speech.

A long time ago I saw the Commander of the Believers ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (may Allah be pleased with him) in a dream and heard him speaking about this question. I think I discussed it with him, and I understood from his words that speaking good is better than keeping silent.
I think that in the course of the conversation Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik was mentioned, and that ʿUmar had said this to him.

It has been narrated that Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik said: Silence is the sleep of the mind and speech its waking, and neither state is complete without the other — meaning that both silence and speech are needed.

How excellent is what ʿUbaydullāh ibn Abī Jaʿfar said — the jurist of the people of Egypt in his time, and one of the wise: When a man is talking in a gathering and his talk pleases him, let him fall silent; and when he is silent

and his silence pleases him, let him talk. This is good, for whoever is like this keeps silent and talks against his own inclination and self-satisfaction, and whoever is like this deserves that Allah should grant him success and keep him on the right course in his speech and his silence,
because both his speech and his silence are for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Among the mursal reports of al-Ḥasan is that the Prophet ﷺ said, in what he narrates from his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic: “The sign of purity is that the servant's heart is attached to Me. When that is so, he does not forget Me in any state;

and when that is so, I favour him with being occupied with Me so that he does not forget Me; and if he forgets Me, I stir his heart. If he speaks, he speaks for Me, and if he is silent, he is silent for Me. That is the one to whom help comes from Me.” Ibrāhīm ibn al-Junayd recorded it.

In any case, binding oneself to total silence, and believing it to be an act that brings one near to Allah, whether in general or in certain acts of worship such as Ḥajj, spiritual retreat (iʿtikāf) and fasting, is forbidden.
It has been narrated, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ forbade the fast of silence.

Al-Ismāʿīlī recorded from the hadith of ʿAlī: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade us silence during spiritual retreat. In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, ʿAlī narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There is no keeping silent for a whole day until night.”
Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) said to a woman who was performing Ḥajj in silence: This is not lawful; this is one of the practices of the Jāhiliyyah.
It has been narrated that ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn said: The fast of silence is unlawful.
The second thing the Prophet ﷺ commanded the believers in this hadith is honouring the neighbour; some narrations have “the prohibition of harming the neighbour”. Harming the neighbour is forbidden;
harming anyone without right is forbidden, but harming a neighbour is forbidden more strictly still. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Ibn Masʿūd narrated that the Prophet ﷺ was asked: Which sin is greatest?
He said: “That you set up a rival to Allah when He created you.” He was asked: Then what?
He said: “That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you.” He was asked: Then what?
He said: “That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife.”
In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad, al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
“What do you say about fornication?” They said:

It is unlawful; Allah and His Messenger have made it unlawful, so it is unlawful until the Day of Resurrection. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “For a man to commit fornication with ten women is lighter for him than to commit it with his neighbour's wife.” He said: “What do you say about theft?”
They said: Allah and His Messenger have made it unlawful, so it is unlawful. He said: “For a man to steal from ten houses is lighter for him than to steal from his neighbour.”

In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Abū Shurayḥ narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “By Allah, he does not believe! By Allah, he does not believe! By Allah, he does not believe!” He was asked: Who, O Messenger of Allah?
He said: “The one whose neighbour is not safe from his harm.”
Imam Aḥmad and others recorded it from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “He will not enter Paradise whose neighbour is not safe from his harm.”
Imam Aḥmad and al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that he said: Someone said:
O Messenger of Allah, a certain woman prays at night and fasts by day, but there is something in her tongue: she is sharp-tongued and harms her neighbours. He said:

“There is no good in her; she is in the Fire.” He was told: A certain woman prays the obligatory prayers, fasts Ramaḍān and gives pieces of dried curd in charity, and has nothing besides, but she harms no one. He said: “She is in Paradise.” Imam Aḥmad's wording is: “and she does not harm her neighbours with her tongue.”
Al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of Abū Juḥayfah, that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining about his neighbour, and he said to him: “Put your belongings out in the road.” The narrator said:

So people began passing by him and cursing [the neighbour]. Then [the neighbour] came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, what I have met with from people! He said: “What have you met with from them?”
He said: They curse me. He said: “Allah cursed you before the people did.” He said: O Messenger of Allah, I will not do it again.
Abū Dāwūd recorded something with the same meaning from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, but did not mention in it: “Allah cursed you before the people did.”

Al-Kharāʾiṭī recorded, from the hadith of Umm Salamah, that she said: A sheep belonging to a neighbour of ours came in and took a round loaf of ours, so I went over to it and pulled it from between its jaws. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “No harm done to a neighbour is a small matter.”
As for honouring the neighbour and treating him well, that is commanded. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has said:

“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, to relatives, orphans and the needy, to the near neighbour and the distant neighbour, to the companion at your side, to the wayfarer, and to those your right hands possess. Allah does not love whoever is arrogant and boastful” [al-Nisāʾ 4:36].

In this verse Allah the Exalted brought together the mention of His own right over the servant and of the rights of His servants over the servant as well, and He made the servants whom He commanded us to treat well of five kinds.
The first: those to whom a person is related by kinship. Among them He singled out parents for mention,

because they are distinguished from all other relatives by something they do not share with them: they were the cause of the child's existence, and theirs is the right of having raised and disciplined him, and more besides.

The second: whoever is weak and in need of kindness. These are of two kinds: one in need because of bodily weakness, who is the orphan, and one in need because of lack of wealth, who is the poor person (miskīn).
The third: those who have a right through nearness and close association. He made them of three kinds: the near neighbour, the distant neighbour, and the companion at one's side.

The exegetes differed over how to interpret this. Some said: The near neighbour is a neighbour who is a relative, and the distant neighbour is one who is not related. Some included the wife under the near neighbour, and some included her under the distant neighbour,

and some included the travelling companion under the distant neighbour. It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ used to say in his supplication: “I seek refuge in You from a bad neighbour in a settled home, for the neighbour in the desert moves on.”
Some said: The near neighbour is the Muslim neighbour, and the distant neighbour is the disbeliever. In the Musnad of al-Bazzār there is, from the hadith of Jābir as marfūʿ:

“Neighbours are of three kinds: a neighbour who has one right, and he is the neighbour with the least right; a neighbour who has two rights; and a neighbour who has three rights, and he is the neighbour with the greatest right.
The one who has one right is an idolater neighbour with no tie of kinship: he has the right of neighbourliness. The one who has two rights is a Muslim neighbour:

he has the right of Islam and the right of neighbourliness. The one who has three rights is a Muslim neighbour who is a relative: he has the right of Islam, the right of neighbourliness and the right of kinship.”
This hadith has also been narrated by other routes, connected and mursal, and none of them is free of criticism.
It has also been said: The near neighbour is the one close by, next door, and the distant neighbour is the one whose house is far off.
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, ʿĀʾishah said: I said: O Messenger of Allah, I have two neighbours; to which of them should I give gifts?
He said: “To the one whose door is nearer to you.”
A group of the Salaf said: Neighbourliness extends to forty houses; it has also been said: to forty houses all around, in every direction.
Among the mursal reports of al-Zuhrī: a man came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining about a neighbour of his, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered one of his Companions to call out: “Forty houses are neighbours!”
Al-Zuhrī said: Forty this way, forty this way, forty this way and forty this way — meaning in front of him, behind him, on his right and on his left.
Imam Aḥmad was asked about someone who cooks a pot while living in a lodging-house (dār al-sabīl) with about thirty or forty people in the house with him — meaning
that they live in the house with him. He said: He begins with himself and his dependants; if anything is left over, he gives it to whoever is closest to him. How could he give to all of them?
He was asked: What if his neighbour thinks little of that potful and it means nothing to him?
He took the view that he need not send any to him.

As for the companion at one's side, one group explained it as the wife, and another group, among them Ibn ʿAbbās, as the travelling companion. They did not mean to exclude the constant companion at home; they meant that if companionship on a journey suffices, then lasting companionship at home has all the more right.

That is why Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: He is the righteous companion; Zayd ibn Aslam said: He is the one who sits with you at home and your companion on a journey; and Ibn Zayd said: He is the man who comes to you and calls on you so that you may benefit him.
In the Musnad and al-Tirmidhī, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“The best of companions in the sight of Allah is the best of them to his companion, and the best of neighbours in the sight of Allah is the best of them to his neighbour.”

The fourth: one who comes to a person without staying with him permanently. This is the wayfarer (ibn al-sabīl), meaning the traveller who arrives in another land. Some explained it as the guest, meaning the wayfarer when he stops as someone's guest.

The fifth: those whom one's right hand possesses. The Prophet ﷺ often gave instructions concerning them and commanded that they be treated well, and it has been narrated that the last thing he enjoined at his death was:
“The prayer, and those your right hands possess.” Some of the Salaf included under this verse the animals and livestock a person owns.

Let us return to the explanation of Abū Hurayrah's hadith on honouring the neighbour. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, ʿĀʾishah and Ibn ʿUmar narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Jibrīl kept enjoining me to treat the neighbour well until I thought he would make him an heir.”
One form of kindness to the neighbour is to help him in his need. In the Musnad, ʿUmar narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The believer does not eat his fill while his neighbour goes without.”
Al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “He is not a believer who eats his fill while his neighbour is hungry.”
In another narration from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said: “He has not believed who spends the night full while his neighbour goes hungry.”
In the Musnad, ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The first two disputants on the Day of Resurrection will be two neighbours.”

In al-Bukhārī's book al-Adab, Ibn ʿUmar narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “How many a neighbour will cling to his neighbour on the Day of Resurrection, saying: My Lord, this man shut his door against me and withheld his kindness!”
Al-Kharāʾiṭī and others recorded, with a weak chain, from the hadith of ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ:
“Whoever shuts his door against his neighbour for fear for his family and property, that one is not a believer; and he is not a believer whose neighbour is not safe from his harm.
Do you know what the neighbour's right is?

When he asks your help, help him; when he asks you for a loan, lend to him; when he becomes poor, come to his aid; when he falls ill, visit him; when good comes to him, congratulate him; when calamity befalls him, console him; when he dies, follow his funeral. Do not build higher than him and block the breeze from him, except with his permission.

Do not trouble him with the smell of your cooking pot unless you ladle some out for him. If you buy fruit, give him some as a gift; if you do not, bring it in secretly, and do not let your child take it out to provoke his child with it.” It is munkar (objectionable) to trace these words back to the Prophet ﷺ; perhaps they are ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī's own explanation.

It has also been narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, from al-Ḥasan, from Jābir, as marfūʿ: “The least of the neighbour's right is that you do not trouble your neighbour with the smell of your cooking pot unless you scoop some out for him.”

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Abū Dharr said: “My dear friend ﷺ instructed me: When you cook broth, add plenty of water to it, then look to the households of your neighbours and give them some of it in a fitting way.”
In one narration, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Abū Dharr, when you cook broth, add plenty of water to it and look after your neighbours.”
In the Musnad and al-Tirmidhī: ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ slaughtered a sheep and said three times: Have you given some of it as a gift to our Jewish neighbour?
Then he said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “Jibrīl kept enjoining me to treat the neighbour well until I thought he would make him an heir.”

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “None of you should forbid his neighbour to fix a beam in his wall.” Then Abū Hurayrah would say: Why do I see you turning away from it? By Allah, I will throw it between your shoulders!
The school of Imam Aḥmad is that a man is obliged to let his neighbour rest his beams on his wall if the neighbour needs to and it does not damage his wall,
because of this authentic hadith. The apparent sense of his words is that he is obliged to help him from the surplus of what he has, in a way that does him no harm, when he knows of his need.
Al-Marrūdhī said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh [Aḥmad]: I hear the beggar in the street saying, "I am hungry." He said: He may be telling the truth, and he may be lying.
I said: What if I have a neighbour whom I know to be going hungry?
He said: You help him. I said: What if my provision is two loaves?
He said: You give him something to eat. Then he said: What has come in the hadith is only about the neighbour.
Al-Marrūdhī said: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh: Is it obligatory for the rich to help others?
He said: When people are piling up one thing on top of another, how could it not be obligatory for them? I said: If a man has two shirts — or I said: two cloaks — is he obliged to help?
He said: If what he has is surplus.

This is an explicit statement from him that helping others from one's surplus is obligatory, and he did not restrict it to the neighbour, whereas his first statement implies that it is restricted to the neighbour.

In the narration of Ibn Hāniʾ he said, about beggars: That they are lying is dearer to us; if they were telling the truth, we would have no choice but to help them. This indicates that it is obligatory to help the hungry, whether neighbours or others.
In the Ṣaḥīḥ, Abū Mūsā narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Feed the hungry, visit the sick and free the captive.”

In the Musnad and the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Ḥākim, Ibn ʿUmar narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Any people of a quarter among whom a man wakes up hungry, the protection of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has been withdrawn from them.”

The school of Aḥmad and Mālik is that a neighbour is prevented from using his own private property in a way that harms his neighbour. In their view it is obligatory to keep harm from the neighbour by preventing any new use that harms him,

even if the one making use of it is only using his own private property. In Aḥmad's view it is also obligatory to give one's neighbour what he needs when giving it does one no harm. Higher than both of these is to bear one's neighbour's harm patiently and not repay it with harm.
Al-Ḥasan said: Good neighbourliness is not refraining from harm; good neighbourliness is bearing harm. It is narrated from the hadith of Abū Dharr, who attributed it to the Prophet ﷺ:
“Allah loves a man who has a neighbour who harms him by his proximity, and he bears his harm patiently until death or departure separates them.” Imam Aḥmad recorded it.

Among the mursal reports of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ḥubulī: a man came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining to him about his neighbour, and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Keep your harm from him and bear his harm patiently; death is enough to separate you.” Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it.
The third thing the Prophet ﷺ commanded the believers is honouring the guest, meaning hosting him well. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the hadith of Abū Shurayḥ, he said:
My eyes saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and my ears heard him when he said it: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest with his due (jāʾizah).” They said: What is his due?
He said: “A day and a night.” He said: “Hospitality is three days, and whatever is after that is charity.”
Muslim also recorded, from the hadith of Abū Shurayḥ, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Hospitality is three days, and his due is a day and a night.

Whatever is spent on him after that is charity. It is not lawful for him to stay on with his host until he makes him fall into sin.” They said: O Messenger of Allah, how would he make him fall into sin?
He said: “He stays with him when he has nothing with which to host him.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest.”
He said it three times. They said: What is the honouring of the guest, O Messenger of Allah?
He said: “Three days; whatever he stays after that is charity.”

These hadiths state that the guest's due is a day and a night and that hospitality is three days, so he distinguished between the due and hospitality and stressed the due. Other hadiths have also come stressing it. Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib,

that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The guest's night is a duty on every Muslim. If the morning finds him in someone's courtyard [unhosted], it is a debt owed to him: if he wishes he may claim it, and if he wishes he may let it go.”
Ibn Mājah recorded it with the wording: “The guest's night is a duty on every Muslim.”

Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd recorded, from the hadith of al-Miqdām, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “If any man comes as a guest to a people and wakes up deprived, every Muslim is duty-bound to help him until he takes the hospitality of one night from their crops and property.”
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir said: We said: O Messenger of Allah, you send us out, and we stop among people who do not host us. What do you think?

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to us: “If you stop among a people and they order for you what is fitting for a guest, accept it; and if they do not, take from them the guest's due that they ought to give.”

Imam Aḥmad and al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Any guest who stops among a people and wakes up deprived may take the equivalent of his hospitality, and there is no blame on him.”
ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr said: Whoever does not host guests is not of Muḥammad, nor of Ibrāhīm.
ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Jazʾ said: Whoever does not honour his guest is not of Muḥammad, nor of Ibrāhīm.

Abū Hurayrah stopped among some people and asked them for hospitality, but they did not host him. So he moved aside and set up camp, and invited them to his food, but they did not accept. He said to them:

You do not host the guest and you do not accept an invitation; you have nothing of Islam! One of them recognised him and said to him: Come and stay, may Allah keep you well. He said: This is evil upon evil: you host only those you know.
Something similar has been narrated of Abū al-Dardāʾ, except that he said to them: You have no more of the religion than this — and he pointed to a loose thread on the edge of his garment.
These texts show that hosting for a day and a night is obligatory. This is the view of al-Layth and Aḥmad. Aḥmad said: The guest may demand it if he is refused,
because it is an obligatory right owed to him. Does he take it with his own hand from the host's property if he is refused, or does he take the matter to the judge?
On this there are two reported positions of Aḥmad, both stated explicitly.

Ḥumayd ibn Zanjawayh said: The guest's night is obligatory, but he may not take his hospitality from them by force, unless he is travelling on the general business of the Muslims and not on his own business.
Al-Layth ibn Saʿd said: If a guest stops with a slave, the slave hosts him from the property in his hands, and the guest may eat even if he does not know that the slave's master has given permission,
because hospitality is obligatory.
This is in keeping with Aḥmad's view,

since he stated explicitly that it is permissible to accept the invitation of a slave who has been permitted to trade. It has been narrated that a number of the Companions accepted the invitations of slaves,

and this has also been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ. If a slave may invite people to his food on his own initiative, and accepting his invitation is permissible, then his hosting someone who stops with him is all the more so.
Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and others did not allow accepting the invitation of a slave permitted to trade without his master's permission. ʿAlī ibn Saʿīd transmitted

from Aḥmad something indicating that hospitality is obligatory only towards those on military campaign, from whoever they pass by, for three days; but the well-known view from him is the first: that it is obligatory towards every guest who stops among a people.
His statements differ on whether it is obligatory on the people of cities as well as villages, or only on the people of villages and those on a road along which travellers pass.
There are two reported positions of his on this, both stated explicitly.

His stated view is that it is obligatory towards both Muslim and disbeliever, but many of his followers restricted the obligation to Muslims, just as maintenance of relatives is not obligatory when they differ in religion, according to one of his two reported positions.
As for the other two days, the second and the third, they complete the hospitality. Aḥmad's stated view is that only the first due (jāʾizah) is obligatory, and he said:

[The Prophet ﷺ] distinguished between the due and hospitality, and the due is the more stressed. Some scholars of our [Ḥanbalī] school held that hospitality for three days is obligatory, among them Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz,
Ibn Abī Mūsā and al-Āmidī; whatever is beyond the three is charity. Some people thought that the hospitality is three days after the first day and night,
and Aḥmad refuted this with his words ﷺ: “Hospitality is three days, and whatever is more is charity”; if it were as this person thought, it would be four.
I say: A parallel to this is the words of the Exalted:

“Say: Do you really disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days…” up to His words: “and blessed it and measured out its sustenance in four days” [Fuṣṣilat 41:9–10]; what is meant is four days in all.
The hadith that Aḥmad cited as proof has already been given from the hadith of Abū Shurayḥ. Al-Bukhārī also recorded it from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah,
from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him host his guest well.” He was asked: O Messenger of Allah, what is the hosting of the guest?
He said: “Three [days]; whatever is after that is charity.”

Ḥumayd ibn Zanjawayh said: For the day and night he must go to the trouble of giving him the best food that he and his family eat, and for the rest of the three he feeds him from his ordinary food. This is questionable.

We shall cite the hadith of Salmān forbidding going to trouble for a guest. Ashhab transmitted that Mālik said: His due is a day and a night, in which he honours him, treats him to something special and attends to him particularly, for a day and a night; and three days are hospitality.
Ibn ʿUmar used to refuse to eat from the property of whoever he was staying with beyond three days, and would give orders that he be provided for from his own wealth.
The householder may tell the guest to move on after the three days,
because he has discharged what he owed. Imam Aḥmad did this.

His words ﷺ, “It is not lawful for him to stay on with him until he causes him difficulty”, mean that he stays with him until he puts him under strain. But does this apply within the three days or beyond them?

As for what is not obligatory, there is no doubt that it is forbidden. As for what is obligatory, namely the day and the night, it depends on whether hospitality is obligatory on someone who has nothing, or only on someone who has the means to host.

If it is said that it is obligatory only on someone who has the means to host — which is the view of a group of hadith scholars, among them Ḥumayd ibn Zanjawayh — then it is not lawful for the guest to seek hospitality from someone unable to provide it.

It has been narrated from the hadith of Salmān: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade us to go to trouble for a guest over what we do not have.” If the host is forbidden to go to trouble for the guest over what he does not have, this shows that he is not obliged to share with the guest except from what he has;
so if he has no surplus, nothing is required of him. As for preferring the guest over oneself, as did the Anṣārī about whom this was revealed:
“They prefer others over themselves, even though they are in want” [al-Ḥashr 59:9] — that is a station of virtue and excellence, not an obligation.

If the guest knew that they would host him only with their own food and their children's food, and that the children would suffer for it, it would not then be permissible for him to seek their hospitality, in keeping with his words ﷺ: “It is not lawful for him to stay on with him until he causes him difficulty.”

Moreover, hospitality is an obligatory expense, so it is obligatory only on someone who has something left over beyond his own provision and that of his dependants, like the maintenance of relatives and zakāt al-fiṭr.

Al-Khaṭṭābī objected to explaining “making him fall into sin” as staying with him when he has nothing with which to host him. He said: I consider it a mistake. How could he fall into sin over this when he cannot afford to host him and has no means of doing so?

Obligation is only according to capacity. He said: The real sense of the hadith is that he disliked his staying with him after three days, lest the host should feel strained by his presence, so that his charity would come with reproach and hurt and his reward would be lost. What he said is questionable,

for the explanation he rejected is given in the hadith itself, and authentically. The real sense is that if the guest stays with him when he has nothing with which to host him, the strain the host feels on his account
may drive him to sin in word or deed. What is meant is not that he sins by not hosting him when he is unable to. And Allah knows best.
